For all the folks having connection issues with the (online) game. Got the following info for you:

- Played this locally on my xbox years ago, worked like a charm because of local.
- Bought it (for my wife and myself) at a recent sale to show her the fun of this game
- Online worked for me in an instant, but struggled to connect on her PC, even when giving permission via epic games (browser-popup)

The solution to all your problems is the following:
It seems to be epic's fault
- Go to your epic games account management site (via browser)
- Unlink steam from epic games
(if you already tried to link TRDS, go to "Apps" and unlink that too)
- go to %localappdata% and delete the webcache folders in your "Epic Games Launcher"-->"Saved" directory if there are any

If epic games wont let you log in, it's their homepage that's bugged. Sad for a company that size.
You can google "epic games manage account" and go there via direct link. You should already be logged in and able to see the "App/Service" section where steam and TRDS are visible.

After all these steps close epic games launcher on your pc (if opened) and log out of your browser session at epic.
Then start TRDS and click "Connect to online services" - a small lag should happen (1 or 2 sec) and voilà, you should be able to see the new online buttons.

A little messy, hope this helps anyone.

PS: Even vsync activated did not work with 120 fps/hz for me. Locked on 60 in the open world. Tutorial works with 120 tho.

Totally Reliable Delivery Service, developed by We’re Five Games and published on Steam by Infogrames and Atari, is a game built entirely around the comedic potential of physics-driven chaos. Instead of aiming for accuracy, precision, or traditional platforming fluidity, it leans enthusiastically into wobbling ragdolls, flimsy vehicles, unpredictable momentum, and spontaneous slapstick failure. The premise appears straightforward—deliver packages across a colorful series of open environments—but the mechanical foundation intentionally turns every delivery attempt into a miniature disaster waiting to unfold. The game’s charm stems not from accomplishing tasks efficiently, but from how spectacularly things fall apart along the way, transforming routine objectives into improvised comedy sketches. Its design philosophy encourages players to abandon expectations of control and embrace the absurdity of its world.

Gameplay revolves around a two-handed grab system that forces players to manually manipulate objects, vehicles, levers, and packages. The controls are intentionally awkward, requiring players to lift and carry objects while balancing weight, momentum, and environmental chaos. Even the simplest actions—opening a door, loading a box into a truck, steering a forklift—become unpredictable and hilarious because the physics refuse to cooperate. Vehicles behave like barely assembled contraptions, wobbling, flipping, or launching into the air with the slightest misjudgment. Rocke
